The Longneck croaker Pseudotolithus typus reaches a maximum recorded total length of 140 centimeters [Li = 140 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger sciaenids inhabiting the coastal waters of the Gulf of Guinea. This ultimate length, documented from surveys of artisanal landings in Ghana and Nigeria, is frequently approached only by the oldest individuals in the population. Hatchlings emerge from demersal eggs that have an estimated wet weight of approximately 0.0001 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0001 grams], a value derived from the mean egg diameter of 0.59 millimeters measured in congeneric species. This diminutive birth mass reflects the typical pattern among marine teleosts that broadcast-spawn large numbers of small, yolk-laden eggs into the plankton. The transition from the lecithotrophic yolk-sac stage to first exogenous feeding represents a critical bottleneck, as the prolarvae must locate suitable prey items within days of mouth opening to avoid starvation. Post-settlement juveniles then recruit to estuarine nursery habitats, where growth accelerates markedly during the first year of life.

Sexual maturation in this species is attained at a total length of 48.3 centimeters [Lp = 48.3 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonad maturation and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Field data from the Ivorian continental shelf indicate that individuals below this length are invariably immature, with no evidence of vitellogenesis or spermiation. The corresponding wet weight at which puberty occurs has been estimated at 940 grams [Wwp = 940 grams], a value consistent with the length-weight relationship established for the species. This body mass is typically reached during the second or third year of life, depending on local productivity regimes and density-dependent competition within nursery estuaries. Interestingly, the onset of reproductive maturity is not strictly size-dependent across all populations; some fish from cooler upwelling zones appear to mature at slightly smaller sizes, suggesting a degree of phenotypic plasticity in response to environmental conditions.

Gravid females of Pseudotolithus typus exhibit a noteworthy spawning strategy when maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a water temperature of 25.7 °C [T = 25.7 °C]. At a standard length of 36 centimeters, mature individuals produce approximately 386 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 386 eggs per day], a reproductive rate that has been extrapolated from detailed fecundity studies on the closely related sciaenid Pseudotolithus senegalensis. This daily output is substantial for a fish of this size and reflects an iteroparous strategy in which multiple spawning events occur throughout an extended breeding season that spans the warmer months. The sustained high rate of oocyte production is energetically demanding and is supported by the rich feeding grounds found in the shallow, productive waters of the continental shelf. Peak spawning activity coincides with elevated prey abundance, ensuring that the exogenously feeding larvae encounter adequate food resources upon yolk-sac resorption.

The maximum lifespan of the Longneck croaker has been determined through otolith increment analysis, with the oldest individuals in the wild reaching approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] of age under the thermal regime typical of tropical West African waters, which averages 25.7 °C [T = 25.7 °C]. This longevity is intermediate among West African sciaenids; it exceeds that of the shorter-lived Pseudotolithus senegalensis but falls considerably short of the croaker Pseudotolithus typus 's congener Pseudotolithus elongatus, which may persist for over 15 years. The life span is likely constrained by a combination of fishing mortality, which selectively removes larger and older individuals, and the high metabolic demands of warm tropical waters, which may accelerate senescence. Despite this apparently moderate maximum age, the species displays a steep decline in somatic growth after the onset of maturity, with most annual length increments after age five being less than 2 percent of the original size.

The asymptotic wet weight, representing the maximum body mass achieved by fully grown adults, has been calculated at 24,398 grams [Wwi = 24,398 grams] based on the length-weight relationship derived from extensive fishery-independent surveys. This corresponds to fish that have attained the species' ultimate total length of 140 centimeters [Li = 140 centimeters], which are predominantly large females in the uppermost size classes. Achieving such a mass requires several years of consistent feeding and favorable environmental conditions, and it is rarely observed in heavily exploited populations where larger individuals are selectively harvested. The bioenergetic demands of maintaining a body this large in a warm-water environment are considerable, and the energetic costs of daily tissue upkeep must be met through a high ingestion rate. Interestingly, the length-weight relationship shows that females tend to be heavier at a given length than males, a pattern attributed to the energetic investments associated with vitellogenesis and the production of large numbers of pelagic oocytes.
